propositions.text: The Lougheed Building was designated a Municipal Historic Resource under the HRA.
LBI was the owner at designation and agreed to rehabilitate the building with restrictions in exchange for 15 yearly Incentive Payments from the City totaling $3.4 million.
The Incentive Payments compensated LBI for restoration and economic value decrease due to designation.
The Incentive Agreement was registered by caveat on title pursuant to the HRA.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Lougheed Building was designated historic, LBI agreed to rehabilitate it for Incentive Payments from the City, and the agreement was registered on title.

propositions.text: The appeal involves a dispute between Heritage (LBI's creditor) and 604 (present owner) over rights to the Incentive Payments.
Whether the Incentive Payments constitute a positive covenant running with the land under the HRA, whether they were sold in the judicial sale, and the effect of assignments.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the dispute between Heritage and 604 over Incentive Payments and the legal issues involved.

propositions.text: Master and chambers judge found Incentive Payments did not run with the land and were not sold to 604.
They declined to decide priority issue.
Court of Appeal majority found HRA creates sui generis covenants displacing common law rule and that Incentive Payments ran with the land.
O'Brien J.A. dissented, supporting chambers judge's interpretation.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports lower courts found Incentive Payments did not run with land; Court of Appeal majority disagreed; O'Brien J.A. dissented.

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed.
Section 29(3) HRA provides covenants related to preservation or restoration run with the land and can be enforced whether positive or negative.
Only covenants in favour of persons or organizations listed in s. 29(1) run with the land under HRA.
Although City is listed, the covenant to pay Incentive Payments is not in its favour, so payments do not run with the land.
The Incentive Agreement shows no intention for Incentive Payments to run with the land.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal, concluding only covenants in favour of listed persons run with land, and Incentive Payments do not run with the land.

propositions.text: Incentive Payments were not sold in the judicial sale of the Lougheed Building.
No indication in sale documents that court intended to sell or 604 intended to buy Incentive Payments.
Granting payments to 604 would create an undeserved windfall and lack commercial rationale.
Incentive Payments were assigned as security; priority governed by PPSA.
Disagreement on PPSA effect will be remitted to master in chambers for priority determination.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Incentive Payments were not sold, awarding them to 604 would be unfair, and priority is governed by PPSA, remitting priority issue.

propositions.text: LBI acquired Lougheed Building in 2003 and owned it at designation as Municipal Historic Resource in 2004.
LBI and City entered Incentive Agreement in 2006 for rehabilitation and 15 annual payments totaling $3.4 million.
Incentive Payments compensate LBI for loss of economic value and rehabilitation expenses.
LBI completed rehabilitation in 2007 and began receiving payments.

paragraphs.summary: The court states LBI acquired the building, it was designated historic, and LBI and City agreed on rehabilitation and payments.

propositions.text: Incentive Agreement imposed restrictions: building use for commercial purposes until all payments made, and maintaining performance space in Grand Theatre.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Incentive Agreement imposed use restrictions on the building.

propositions.text: Incentive Agreement was registered by caveat on title as stipulated in clause 8.3.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Incentive Agreement was registered by caveat on title.

propositions.text: In 2006, LBI borrowed from Equitable secured by mortgage, security agreement, and assignments including Incentive Agreement.
In 2007, LBI obtained financing from Heritage and assigned Incentive Payments as security.
LBI defaulted in 2009; Equitable commenced enforcement action; building advertised for judicial sale in 2010.
604's parent company offered to buy building in 2010; offer accepted by court order.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes LBI's loans from Equitable and Heritage, default, judicial sale, and 604's purchase offer.

propositions.text: LBI applied to master for declaration that Incentive Payments were not interest in land or included in sale to 604.
Master adjourned application without decision, allowing sale to close without prejudice to rights on payments.
After closing, Equitable assigned its interest in Incentive Agreement to 604; Heritage Assignment registered later.
No evidence 604 Assignment was registered before Heritage Assignment.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts LBI's application to master, adjournment, post-sale assignments, and registration timing.

propositions.text: 604 submits it is subject to covenants restricting building use and that Incentive Payments run with the land under HRA registration.
Alternatively, 604 argues Incentive Payments were sold in judicial sale.

paragraphs.summary: 604 argues it is bound by covenants and entitled to Incentive Payments as running with land or sold in judicial sale.

propositions.text: Heritage and LBI argue HRA does not allow Incentive Payments to run with land; payments are contractual and not intended to run.
They argue payments were not sold in judicial sale.
Heritage claims priority under PPSA as creditor with first registered security.

paragraphs.summary: Heritage and LBI argue payments do not run with land, were not sold, and Heritage has priority under PPSA.

propositions.text: Master Laycock declared Incentive Payments not an interest in land.
HRA requires City to compensate owner at time of designation.
Parties intended payments as purely contractual benefit to LBI.
Payments were not sold to 604 in judicial sale.
No indication in sale documents that payments were included.

paragraphs.summary: Master found payments not interest in land, intended as contractual benefit, and not sold to 604.

propositions.text: No mention of payments in 604 Offer or court acceptance.
Equitable's claim referred to general security but payments not included.
604 Assignment executed after sale was ineffective as debt not transferred.

paragraphs.summary: Master found payments not included in sale offer or claim and 604 Assignment ineffective post-sale.

propositions.text: Chambers judge dismissed 604's appeal, declaring LBI entitled to payments as of August 30, 2010.
s.29(3) HRA does not allow positive covenants to run with land except in favour of City.
HRA scheme requires City to compensate owner at designation time.
Parties did not intend payments to run with land.
Judicial sale offer did not expressly include payments.
Declined to decide PPSA priority issue as 604 Assignment executed after August 30, 2010.

paragraphs.summary: Chambers judge upheld master, found payments did not run with land, not included in sale, and declined PPSA priority decision.

propositions.text: Standard of review for chambers judge's interpretation is correctness.
HRA creates sui generis historic resource covenant running fully with land.
s.29 displaces common law rule prohibiting positive covenants running with land.
Incentive Agreement cannot be severed to separate payments from building obligations.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal majority found standard of review correctness, HRA creates covenants running with land, and payments inseparable from obligations.

propositions.text: Omission of Incentive Agreement in Equitable's claim does not imply forgoing security.
Receivership order included Incentive Agreement.
604 took title subject to caveat protecting historic covenants.
Payments conditional on performance of obligations; burdens and benefits passed with sale.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal majority found payments inseparable from burdens, 604 took title subject to covenants, and payments passed with sale.

propositions.text: Interpretation of HRA and common law principles is correctness standard; application and interpretation of agreements is palpable and overriding error standard.
HRA ensures covenants in favour of City run with land; does not permit positive covenants in favour of landowner to run.
Parties did not intend Incentive Payments to run with land.

paragraphs.summary: O'Brien J.A. dissented, applying mixed standards of review and finding payments do not run with land.

propositions.text: Incentive Agreement not included in 604 Offer; no indication payments included in sale documents.
Court of Appeal not in position to determine entitlement to payments at that time.

paragraphs.summary: O'Brien J.A. found payments not included in sale and Court of Appeal could not decide entitlement.

propositions.text: What is the standard of review for chambers judge's interpretation of Incentive Agreement and 604 Offer?
Did Incentive Payments run with the land?
Does s.29 of HRA displace common law rule on positive covenants?
Does Incentive Agreement show intention for payments to run with land?
Were Incentive Payments sold as asset in judicial sale?
Is priority of interests governed by PPSA?

paragraphs.summary: The court lists four main issues: standard of review, whether payments run with land, sale inclusion, and PPSA priority.

propositions.text: Contractual interpretation involves mixed fact and law, applying principles to contract words in factual context (Sattva, para. 50)
Deference to fact finders limits appeals and promotes trial autonomy, favoring deference on contractual interpretation (Sattva, paras. 50-52)

paragraphs.summary: The court states contractual interpretation involves mixed fact and law and deference to fact finders is appropriate (Sattva, Rothstein J.).

propositions.text: Correctness standard applies to extricable questions of law like incorrect principles or failure to consider legal elements (Sattva, para. 53)

paragraphs.summary: The court states correctness standard applies to extricable legal questions, including misapplication of legal principles (Sattva, Rothstein J.).

propositions.text: 604 submits chambers judge erred interpreting HRA, tainting Incentive Agreement and 604 Offer interpretation, requiring correctness standard
Disagrees; correctness standard applies to HRA statutory interpretation but not to contractual interpretation of Incentive Agreement and 604 Offer
Chambers judge's interpretation of HRA was correct and did not taint contractual interpretation

paragraphs.summary: 604 argues chambers judge erred on HRA affecting contract interpretation standard; court disagrees, finding HRA interpretation correct and no taint.

propositions.text: O’Brien J.A. correctly applied correctness standard to HRA and common law interpretation
Palpable and overriding error standard applies to chambers judge’s interpretation of Incentive Agreement and 604 Offer

paragraphs.summary: The court finds O’Brien J.A. correctly applied correctness to HRA/common law and palpable error to contractual interpretation.

propositions.text: Payment obligations running with land are unusual; common law disallows positive covenants running with land (Austerberry)
Common law rule: positive covenants cannot run with land, even with express contrary intention (Amberwood)
Rule based on contract liability only for parties (Rhone v. Stephens)
Common law rule: no personal or affirmative covenant requiring money or acts runs with land absent statute (Di Castri, Westbank)
Issue is whether s. 29 of HRA displaces common law rule allowing positive covenants to run with land

paragraphs.summary: The court explains common law disallows positive covenants running with land and frames issue whether HRA s.29 displaces this rule.

propositions.text: O’Brien J.A. and chambers judge properly interpreted HRA s.29
Section 29 limits positive covenants running with land to those in favour of entities listed in s.29(1) and enforceable by them
HRA does not permit positive covenants in favour of entities not listed in s.29(1) to run with land

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s.29 limits positive covenants running with land to those enforceable by entities listed in s.29(1).

propositions.text: Modern statutory interpretation requires reading s.29 in context, ordinary sense, harmoniously with Act's scheme and purpose (Sullivan, Bell ExpressVu, Doe, CN Railway)
Only covenants in favour of persons or organizations listed in s.29(1), positive or negative, run with land
In this case, Incentive Payments did not become interest running with land by virtue of HRA

paragraphs.summary: The court applies modern statutory interpretation to conclude only covenants in favour of s.29(1) entities run with land; Incentive Payments do not.

propositions.text: Statutory provisions are presumed to work together as parts of a functioning whole, forming an internally consistent framework (Sullivan, Côté)

paragraphs.summary: The court states statutes are presumed internally consistent and provisions work together as a whole (Sullivan, Côté).

propositions.text: Legislative exceptions to common law should be narrowly construed absent clear, unambiguous intention to change law (Parry Sound, Goodyear, Slaight)

paragraphs.summary: The court cites presumption that legislative exceptions to common law are narrowly construed unless clearly intended otherwise.

propositions.text: Legislation must clearly and unambiguously intend to alter common law to do so (Sullivan quoting Halsbury’s)

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Sullivan that statutes should not alter common law unless clearly and unambiguously intended.

propositions.text: Exception in s.29 HRA to common law rule should be limited by precise language and HRA purpose
Section 29 should not be interpreted more broadly than necessary
Positive covenants run with land only if enforceable by entities listed in s.29(1)
Purposive and contextual analysis shows HRA does not have broader reach by necessary implication

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s.29 exception to common law is limited to entities listed and should not be broadly interpreted.

propositions.text: HRA s.2 assigns Minister responsibility for coordination, preservation, study, interpretation, and promotion of Alberta’s historic resources
Historic resource defined broadly including palaeontological, archaeological, historic, cultural, natural, scientific, or esthetic interest (s.1(e))

paragraphs.summary: The court states HRA s.2 assigns Minister duties and defines historic resource broadly (s.1(e)).

propositions.text: Municipality may designate historic resource by bylaw (s.26(2))
If bylaw decreases economic value, owner entitled to compensation (s.28(1))
Section 28 does not specify compensation right for future owners nor refer to s.29, supporting chambers judge’s interpretation that compensation is for owner at designation time

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s.26 and s.28 provide for designation and compensation to owner at designation time, supporting chambers judge.

propositions.text: Section 29(1) allows registration of preservation/restoration covenants between owner and Minister, municipality council, Foundation, or approved historical organization
Registrar must endorse memorandum of such covenant on title (s.29(2))
Registered covenant runs with land and can be enforced by listed person/organization regardless of interest in land (s.29(3))
Registered covenant may be assigned to other listed persons/organizations who may enforce it (s.29(4))
Minister may discharge or modify registered covenant by order if in public interest (s.29(5))

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes s.29 provisions on registration, enforcement, assignment, and Minister’s power to modify covenants.

propositions.text: Chambers judge’s interpretation of s.29 provision is correct and accepted by O’Brien J.A.
Sections 29(1) and (3) together allow registration and enforcement of preservation/restoration covenants by listed entities
Without s.29(1) and (3), City could not enforce such covenants at common law due to lack of interest

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with chambers judge and O’Brien J.A. that s.29 allows listed entities to register and enforce covenants.

propositions.text: Section 29(3) does not expressly grant landowner enforcement rights against City
604 argues express language unnecessary as landowner can enforce covenants due to interest in land
Court finds legislature would have expressly said if intending to create covenants enforceable by both City and landowner

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s.29(3) does not grant landowner enforcement rights; 604 argues otherwise but court disagrees.

propositions.text: 604 argues s.29(2) allows owner to register covenants and thus enforce them under HRA despite no express wording in s.29(3)
Court rejects argument; s.29(3) read conjunctively limits enforcement to persons/organizations listed in s.29(1)
Covenant in s.29(3) is same throughout; enforcement is by listed persons/organizations only

paragraphs.summary: 604 argues owner can enforce covenants via s.29(2); court rejects, reading s.29(3) as limiting enforcement to listed entities.

propositions.text: Subsections following s.29(3) confirm court’s interpretation

paragraphs.summary: The court finds subsections after s.29(3) confirm its interpretation.

propositions.text: Section 29(4) allows assignment of registered covenants by listed persons/organizations to others listed in s.29(1)
No mention of landowner’s ability to assign covenants in s.29(4)

paragraphs.summary: The court notes s.29(4) allows assignment only by listed persons/organizations, not landowners.

propositions.text: Section 29 intended to permit governments/public interest bodies without land interest to enforce covenants in their favour
Legislature avoids superfluous words and courts should avoid interpretations rendering statute meaningless or redundant (Sullivan, Attorney General of Quebec, Proulx)
Section 29(4) ensures City can assign covenants to others listed in s.29(1) who may enforce them as original parties

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s.29 allows governments/public bodies to enforce covenants and assigns meaning to all provisions avoiding redundancy.

propositions.text: Minister may discharge or modify a covenant under s. 29(5) if in public interest, but only if covenant is in favour of a person or organization under s. 29(1).
It would be unjust if Minister could unilaterally discharge a covenant to pay in favour of a landowner just by public interest.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 29(5) allows Minister to discharge covenants only if in favour of persons under s. 29(1), rejecting unilateral discharge to landowners.

propositions.text: Sections 29(3), (4), and (5) show only covenants in favour of persons or organizations in s. 29(1) can be enforced under s. 29(3).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds only covenants in favour of persons listed in s. 29(1) are enforceable under s. 29(3).

propositions.text: Incentive Agreement does not show intention that Incentive Payments run with the land; 604's claim fails even if common law rule circumvented.
No basis to disturb chambers judge's findings on contractual interpretation of Incentive Agreement, accepted by O'Brien J.A.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Incentive Agreement does not intend payments to run with land and upholds chambers judge's contractual interpretation.

propositions.text: Clauses 5.3, 8.3, and 8.8 of Incentive Agreement are primarily at issue.
Clause 5.3 allows City to set off unpaid taxes by owner or future owner against amounts owed to owner by City.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies clauses 5.3, 8.3, and 8.8 as key and describes clause 5.3's set-off provision.

propositions.text: Chambers judge concluded clause 5.3 does not intend Incentive Payments to go to future owner.
Clause 5.3 only references future owners regarding payment of taxes, not payment from City.
No palpable and overriding error in chambers judge's interpretation of clause 5.3.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with chambers judge that clause 5.3 does not intend payments to future owners and finds no error in that interpretation.

propositions.text: Chambers judge found clause 8.3 restates s. 29 of HRA about enforcement by City of covenants in its favour.
No palpable and overriding error in chambers judge's interpretation of clause 8.3.
Reference to s. 29 does not show parties intended Incentive Payments to run with the land.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no error in chambers judge's interpretation that clause 8.3 restates s. 29 and does not show payments run with land.

propositions.text: Master found 604, a subsequent owner, is not an administrator, successor or assign of LBI under clause 8.8.
Court agrees 'successor' means corporate successor, distinct from 'successors in title' and 'subsequent owners'.
Contracting parties are presumed to intend legal consequences of their words (G. R. Hall, Canadian Contractual Interpretation Law).
Different terms in clauses 8.3 and 8.8 have distinct meanings; intention was LBI alone entitled to Incentive Payments after rehabilitation.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with master that 604 is not a successor under clause 8.8 and that LBI alone was entitled to payments.

propositions.text: 604 argues it is illogical to sever benefits (payments) from burdens (restrictions) under Incentive Agreement.
Court finds nothing unusual about severing Incentive Payments from burdens related to building's historic designation.

paragraphs.summary: 604 argues benefits and burdens should not be severed; court disagrees and finds severance reasonable.

propositions.text: Clause 5.3 does not confirm payments intended for future owner; reasonable interpretation is payments intended for LBI.
Recitals and clauses 3, 4, and 5.4 support conclusion that LBI entitled to all Incentive Payments.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds clauses and recitals show payments intended for LBI, not future owners.

propositions.text: LBI was owner at designation, completed rehabilitation, suffered loss, and paid for work 604 benefits from.
604 could consider designation when purchasing; payments to future owner would lack commercial rationale and give 604 undeserved windfall.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds LBI was rightful owner entitled to payments and that payments to 604 would be unjustified windfall.

propositions.text: 604 submits it purchased right to Incentive Payments in judicial sale.
Court disagrees; chambers judge's conclusion that payments were not sold is well supported by evidence.

paragraphs.summary: 604 claims it bought payments in judicial sale; court disagrees and supports chambers judge's conclusion.

propositions.text: 604 Offer defines 'Property' as Lougheed Building's legal description (real property) alone.
604 Offer includes ancillary property: fixtures, equipment, chattels owned by vendor, excluding tenant property.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes 604 Offer defines property as real property plus some ancillary fixtures and chattels.

propositions.text: 604 Offer para. 6 states assignable leases and contracts shall be assigned to purchaser, who assumes obligations.
604 argues Incentive Agreement was assignable contract under para. 6 and thus sold to 604 in judicial sale.

paragraphs.summary: 604 argues Incentive Agreement was assignable contract under para. 6 and sold to it in judicial sale.

propositions.text: Chambers judge accepted Incentive Agreement was assignable contract but not sold to 604; para. 6 covers only contracts ancillary to property.
Para. 6 does not expand 'Property' scope; it addresses transaction process.
If 604 intended to buy payments, offer would expressly mention them in property definition or ancillary list.

paragraphs.summary: Chambers judge found para. 6 covers only ancillary contracts and payments not sold to 604; no express mention in offer.

propositions.text: No palpable and overriding error in chambers judge's interpretation limiting para. 6 to ancillary contracts.
Heritage argues 604 did not purchase all assignable contracts, only those ancillary to real property.
Given payments' value, if 604 intended to buy them, offer would state so; no indication it did.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees with chambers judge and Heritage that 604 did not buy payments; no express indication in offer.

propositions.text: Statement of claim for sale did not mention Incentive Agreement or payments.
Judicial sale listing and marketing brochure did not indicate payments included in sale.
O'Brien J.A. observed absence of mention supports chambers judge's conclusion.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes no mention of payments in sale documents, supporting chambers judge's conclusion.

propositions.text: Determine if assignment of Incentive Payments governed by PPSA, given payments not running with land or sold to 604.
LBI assigned Incentive Agreement to Equitable and Heritage before default; 604 Assignment executed after sale.
604 Assignment registered after Heritage Assignment at Personal Property Registry.

paragraphs.summary: Court must decide if PPSA governs Incentive Payments, noting LBI assigned payments to Equitable and Heritage before 604's assignment.

propositions.text: Master Laycock held 604 Assignment ineffective for lack of consideration.
Jeffrey J. declined to decide assignment and redemption issues, viewing them beyond court's scope.
Court of Appeal majority held payments ran with land, so PPSA did not apply.
O'Brien J.A. said Court of Appeal could not determine entitlement due to evidentiary and scope limits.

paragraphs.summary: Master found 604 Assignment ineffective; Jeffrey J. declined to decide; Court of Appeal majority held PPSA inapplicable; O'Brien J.A. noted evidentiary limits.

propositions.text: Heritage argues its assignment registered before 604's, so it has priority under PPSA.
604 replies Equitable Assignment was registered before 604's assignment.
Heritage says if Court declines PPSA issue, it should at least decide if payments are chose in action for further proceedings.

paragraphs.summary: Heritage argues priority under PPSA; 604 replies Equitable registered first; Heritage seeks ruling on chose in action if PPSA issue declined.

propositions.text: PPSA applies to every transaction creating a security interest regardless of form or title to collateral (s. 3(1)(a)).
Incentive Payments are a chose in action, contractual rights not running with land or ancillary to real property.
Interests in Incentive Payments are not exempt from PPSA under s. 4(f) or (g); PPSA governs priority of interests.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes Incentive Payments are chose in action governed by PPSA, not exempt, so PPSA governs priority of interests.

propositions.text: Clause 7 of the Equitable Assignment states it was given by LBI to secure repayment of its mortgage to Equitable
Jeffrey J. held the Equitable Assignment was only a security interest
O’Brien J.A. accepted Jeffrey J.’s conclusion that the assignment was for securing the mortgage debt and was only a security interest

paragraphs.summary: The court states Clause 7 shows the Equitable Assignment secured LBI's mortgage; Jeffrey J. and O’Brien J.A. found it was only a security interest.

propositions.text: The right to Incentive Payments arose only upon LBI’s completion of rehabilitation work
Incentive Payments aimed to satisfy compensation rights from historic designation and restoration
Incentive Payments were one-time to the owner of a newly designated building and not meant to follow the property
Parties agree if Incentive Payments were lump sum, 604 would not recover part of that sum
The court is satisfied the PPSA applies to the Incentive Payments

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Incentive Payments arise after rehabilitation, are one-time, and concludes PPSA applies to them.

propositions.text: Disagreements about assignments and priorities will be remitted to a master in chambers for decision
Equitable Assignment created only a security interest, so Equitable could transfer only its security interest to 604
This Court’s reasons in Krayzel Corp. v. Equitable Trust Co. must be considered in further proceedings on Incentive Payments

paragraphs.summary: The court will remit priority disputes to a master, notes Equitable Assignment gave only a security interest, and references related case Krayzel.

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed and the master in chambers’ order restored, with costs to Heritage and LBI against 604
Incentive Payments under the Incentive Agreement are not an interest in land under the HRA and not assets sold to 604
Disputes about priority under PPSA between Heritage Assignment and 604 Assignment will be remitted to a master in chambers
Appeal allowed with costs
Solicitors for appellant are Burnet, Duckworth & Palmer, Calgary
Solicitors for respondents Lougheed Block Inc. et al. are Willow Park Law Office, Calgary
Solicitors for respondent 604 1st Street S.W. Inc. are Gowling WLG (Canada) Inc., Calgary

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal, restores the master’s order, finds Incentive Payments not land interests, remits priority disputes, and lists solicitors.
